THOUGHT: The patient is a man in his late 40s with a 10‑year, bilateral, progressive loss of acuity and visual fields, symmetric exam (no APD) and severe constriction on Goldmann perimetry. Fundus autofluorescence shows multiple round, distinct hyperautofluorescent foci (fleck‑like), and OCT demonstrates discrete ovoid hyporeflective areas with hyperreflective borders at the level of the outer retina/RPE. Those imaging findings are most consistent with lipofuscin‑laden flecks/subretinal deposits seen in macular dystrophies—classically Stargardt disease (fundus flavimaculatus). The chronic bilateral course, symmetric advanced central visual loss, hyperautofluorescent flecks, and the OCT appearance (ovoid subretinal/RPE lesions with hyperreflective edges) strongly favor an ABCA4‑related macular dystrophy (Stargardt) or closely related pattern dystrophies. Age is a little older than classic juvenile Stargardt but adult‑onset variants are well described. Differential diagnoses that can produce hyperautofluorescent ovoid lesions or drusenoid/subretinal deposits include adult‑onset vitelliform dystrophy / Best‑related variants, multifocal pattern dystrophy of the RPE, and drusenoid AMD; peripheral field constriction raises consideration of more generalized chorioretinal dystrophies (RP/choroideremia/gyrate atrophy), but those are less consistent with the described FAF/OCT morphology. Further confirmatory testing would include dark‑choroid on fluorescein/ICG angiography (historically), fundus autofluorescence pattern mapping, electroretinography (full‑field and multifocal), and targeted genetic testing for ABCA4 and other macular dystrophy genes.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Stargardt disease / Fundus flavimaculatus (ABCA4‑associated macular dystrophy) — most likely
2. Adult‑onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy (AOFVD) / Best‑related vitelliform variant
3. Pattern dystrophy of the RPE (multifocal pattern dystrophy) 
4. Age‑related macular degeneration with drusenoid deposits / early geographic atrophy (less likely given age but imaging can overlap)
5. Generalized chorioretinal dystrophy causing peripheral constriction (e.g., retinitis pigmentosa, choroideremia, gyrate atrophy) — less likely given the characteristic hyperautofluorescent flecks and OCT appearance but included because of the severe field constriction.
